spans.note: team name and blank space on title page
paper title stating the research question
restates the research question about referees, red cards and skin tone

spans.assertion: used a generalized linear mixed effects model (GLMM) to model each player's probability of receiving a red card
the darkest-skin-toned players have a 1.5 times higher risk of a red card than the lightest-skin-toned players (OR=1.48, 95% CI [1.20;1.84])
referees showed considerable variability in their susceptibility to skin tone
referee variability in skin-tone susceptibility could not be explained by the average implicit or explicit racial biases of their countries of origin
dark-skin-toned players received 1.5 times more red cards than light-skin-toned players
this effect could not be explained by the average racial biases of the referees' countries
all calculations were performed in R using the lme4, party, and psych packages
published the full analysis script in an online OSF appendix
removed all participants without a skin tone rating, assuming the data were missing completely at random
removing participants without skin tone ratings reduced the data set by 14.7% to 124,621 unique player-referee dyads
averaged the two raters' skin tone ratings into a single score
inter-rater reliability of the skin tone ratings was ICC(2,k)=.96
coded the skin tone scale to run from 0 (lightest) to 1 (darkest)
did not remove players with missing position data
coded missing player positions as an 'unknown' category
deviation-coded the position variable so each position is compared to the grand mean, with the intercept representing the average position
selected the four most frequent referee countries (Germany, England, France, Spain), covering 61.3% of dyads, out of 161 total countries
assigned referees from all other countries to an 'other country' category
deviation-coded the referee country categorical variable
z-standardized the explicit and implicit bias scores of the referee countries
used binary classification trees from the party package to explore potential covariates and their interactions

spans.note: generic explanation of how binary classification trees work

spans.assertion: the party package's method automatically corrects for multiple testing and bounds the combined Type-I error rate
did not consider it necessary to cross-validate the classification tree results in a fresh data set

found clear main effects of position and referee country, plus a potentially meaningful referee-country-by-skin-tone interaction (relevant for German, English, and other referees but not French or Spanish)

spans.note: notes the classification tree does not account for the data's multilevel structure

spans.assertion: did not treat the country-by-skin-tone interaction from the classification tree as conclusive
used the classification tree as a hypothesis-generating tool, with the hypotheses formally tested later
included main effects for position, referee country, and skin tone plus a skin-tone-by-referee-country interaction term in the final models, based on the exploratory analysis
the exploratory analysis included skin tone, position, standardized implicit and explicit bias, referee country, goals, yellow cards, yellow-red cards, age, and games played
the data set has a cross-classified nested structure (referees met multiple players and players met multiple referees), potentially introducing non-independence
decided to use a multilevel logistic regression model with random intercepts for players and referees, estimated with lme4
the random referee intercept models variability in referee leniency and the random player intercept models variability in players' propensity to get a red card
defined the outcome variable as a binary indicator of whether a player received a red card in a unique player-referee encounter
used skin tone as the focal RQ1 predictor with position and referee country as covariates, and added implicit/explicit bias and their interaction with skin tone for RQ2
model m0 (baseline) included position and referee country as fixed effects plus random intercepts for player and referee
model m1 added skin tone as a fixed-effect predictor (later allowed to vary randomly by referee), serving as the main RQ1 model
model m1b added an interaction between skin tone and referee country, based on the exploratory results
model m2a extended m1 with a main effect of implicit racial bias and its interaction with skin tone, to test RQ2a
model m2b extended m1 with a main effect of explicit racial bias and its interaction with skin tone, to test RQ2b
compared models using chi-square likelihood-ratio tests and delta AICc
all reported confidence intervals are 95% CIs computed with the Wald method
added a random slope allowing the skin tone effect to vary between referees, based on a suggestion from the feedback round
including the random skin-tone slope did not change the model's conclusions

spans.note: cites a recommendation (Barr et al., 2013) to generally include random slopes of focal predictors

spans.assertion: in the initial approach, split the data set into a training set and a validation set
skipped the cross-validation train/validation step because it was deemed unnecessary with the party package
the referee-country-by-skin-tone interaction (model m1b) did not improve the model (Δχ²(4)=3.48, p=.482; ΔAICc=4.53)
discarded the model with the referee-country-by-skin-tone interaction

spans.note: points the reader to Table 1 for parameter estimates

spans.assertion: German and English referees gave fewer red cards than average, and Spanish referees gave more
the center-back position receives more red cards than average, while some positions (e.g., attacking or right midfielder) receive fewer
the skin tone predictor in model m1 has a significant positive slope of 0.40 [0.18;0.61], improving fit over baseline model m0 (Δχ²(3)=11.85, p=.008; ΔAICc=-5.85)
darker-skinned players have a higher probability of receiving a red card
the skin tone effect size expressed as an odds ratio is 1.48 [1.20;1.84]
this OR corresponds to a probability increase from 0.28% (lightest skin tone) to 0.42% (darkest skin tone) for an average position and country
found no evidence that referee countries' average implicit or explicit racial biases modulated the skin tone effect (RQ2)
there is more random-intercept variance between players (0.28) than between referees (0.16)
there is variance of 0.03 in the skin-tone slope across referees
the skin-tone slopes of 90% of referees are estimated to fall between 0.10 and 0.69
individual differences among referees in susceptibility to skin tone cannot be explained by country of origin or by that country's implicit/explicit biases
the analyses revealed strong evidence for a skin tone effect, with darker players receiving more red cards than lighter players
in raw probability terms the effect looks very small because red cards are rare events
in relative-probability terms, the darkest players have a 1.5 times higher red-card risk than the lightest players

spans.note: cautious about drawing causal conclusions given the non-experimental nature of the data
speculates the effect could stem from referee bias or from different playing styles possibly tied to genetic, cultural, or group-dynamic factors
